metadata.summary: This task force report establishes literature-guided, expert-consensus criteria for using multimodal imaging to diagnose and monitor multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS). It describes findings across fundus photography, optical coherence tomography, fundus autofluorescence, fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography, and optical coherence tomography angiography, including features that help distinguish MEWDS from other posterior uveitic conditions. Its criteria focus primarily on primary MEWDS; the report states that evidence is insufficient for definitive imaging recommendations for secondary MEWDS.

target_population: Patients undergoing evaluation for suspected MEWDS

recommendations.statement: Use CFP to record the distribution and location of lesions in MEWDS.
recommendations.rationale: CFP can show the characteristic spots and their distribution across the fundus.
recommendations.source_heading: TABLE 3. Consensus-Based Guidelines for Imaging in Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome

recommendations.statement: Use high-resolution CFP to assess whether foveal granularity is present in active MEWDS.
recommendations.rationale: Foveal granularity can be difficult to discern without high-resolution fundus imaging.
recommendations.source_heading: TABLE 3. Consensus-Based Guidelines for Imaging in Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome

recommendations.statement: Use OCT to diagnose active MEWDS by identifying changes in the outer photoreceptor layers.
recommendations.rationale: Active disease produces multifocal EZ/IZ abnormalities that OCT can detect.
recommendations.source_heading: TABLE 3. Consensus-Based Guidelines for Imaging in Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome

recommendations.statement: Use OCT to exclude active MEWDS when significant choroidal involvement is present.
recommendations.rationale: MEWDS does not typically produce choroidal changes on OCT.
recommendations.source_heading: TABLE 3. Consensus-Based Guidelines for Imaging in Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome

recommendations.statement: Use FAF, including ultra-wide field FAF, when diagnosing MEWDS, while accounting for differences between FAF wavelengths.
recommendations.rationale: FAF detects characteristic spots more sensitively than CFP, but their appearance can vary with the imaging wavelength.
recommendations.source_heading: TABLE 3. Consensus-Based Guidelines for Imaging in Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome

recommendations.statement: Use FFA to document the characteristic individual wreath-like lesions during the mid-phase of active MEWDS.
recommendations.rationale: In the mid-phase, individual lesions show a hypofluorescent center encircled by hyperfluorescence.
recommendations.source_heading: TABLE 3. Consensus-Based Guidelines for Imaging in Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome

recommendations.statement: Use ICGA to distinguish MEWDS from other non-infectious posterior uveitis when the diagnosis is challenging.
recommendations.rationale: Prominent hypofluorescent lesions in early ICGA frames due to choriocapillaris non-perfusion are typical of placoid chorioretinopathies and exclude MEWDS.
recommendations.source_heading: TABLE 3. Consensus-Based Guidelines for Imaging in Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome

recommendations.statement: Use OCTA to document preserved flow signal in the retinal and choriocapillaris slabs in active MEWDS.
recommendations.rationale: A substantial reduction in choriocapillaris OCTA signal favors placoid-type conditions rather than MEWDS.
recommendations.source_heading: TABLE 3. Consensus-Based Guidelines for Imaging in Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome

recommendations.statement: Use OCT and FAF for serial monitoring of MEWDS.
recommendations.rationale: The characteristic OCT abnormalities and hyperautofluorescent lesions diminish as the disease resolves.
recommendations.source_heading: TABLE 3. Consensus-Based Guidelines for Imaging in Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome

conditions.name: primary MEWDS
conditions.description: An ocular condition predominantly affecting the outer retina, with multifocal lesions that usually resolve spontaneously. Its cause remains uncertain; a post-viral immune response or an autoinflammatory process has been proposed.
conditions.epidemiology: The reported incidence of MEWDS is approximately 0.22 per 100,000 people per year. It predominantly affects young women, without a significant racial or ethnic predilection. Approximately half of affected individuals recall a flu-like illness before onset.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Disease is typically unilateral, with deep gray-white outer retinal spots that may coalesce and foveal granularity. Anterior chamber and vitreous inflammation is absent or mild. An enlarged blind spot may correspond to peripapillary retinal changes, and optic disc blurring may occur. Lesions usually fade without intervention, with normal or near-normal visual acuity returning within about 2 to 3 months. Recurrence is possible but rare; approximately 95% of patients attain visual acuity of 20/25 or better after the acute phase. Bilateral presentation is very atypical and warrants consideration of a masquerading or secondary condition, although the task force does not regard bilaterality alone as excluding the diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess laterality, foveal granularity, and the degree of anterior chamber and vitreous inflammation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The SUN classification criteria include multifocal deep retinal spots with foveal granularity and absent-to-mild anterior chamber and vitreous inflammation. Those criteria treat simultaneous bilateral onset as nearly excluding MEWDS; the task force instead emphasizes imaging findings and notes that bilateral cases have been reported.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Record lesion distribution and assess foveal granularity using high-resolution images.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Faint, deep gray-yellow-white spots, typically 50-200 µm, can extend centrifugally from the posterior pole into the midperiphery or cluster around the optic disc or macula. Lesions can merge and fade over days to weeks. High-resolution imaging helps reveal unilateral foveal granularity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify active outer photoreceptor layer abnormalities and assess for substantial choroidal involvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For diagnosis of active disease and serial follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Multifocal, focally hyporeflective disruption of the EZ/IZ can coexist with hyperreflective “puff balls” or pillars extending into the outer retina. Foveal and peripapillary involvement may occur. The ELM can be preserved or attenuated; occasional vertical foveal hyperreflectivity, vitreous hyperreflective foci, nerve fiber layer thickening, or peripapillary serous elevations are described. Changes in the RPE, choriocapillaris, or choroid are not typical; substantial choroidal involvement argues against active MEWDS. Rare RPE irregularities may occur in recurrent cases.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide additional detail and support a diagnosis otherwise achievable with OCT B-scans.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When further imaging detail or diagnostic confirmation is useful.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: EZ- and IZ-level images can show hyporeflective spots corresponding to EZ loss, with overlying hyperreflective dots. Spots, followed by dots, diminish as the condition resolves.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly during the very acute phase.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Wreath-shaped hyporeflective lesions measuring 50-200 µm may be visible.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect characteristic lesions for diagnosis and monitor their resolution.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnosis and serial follow-up, with attention to variation between imaging wavelengths.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Short-wavelength blue or green FAF, described at 488 and 530 nm, is more sensitive than CFP for characteristic spots but can be unremarkable very early. Acute disease shows hyperautofluorescent spots with overlying dots; spots resolve before dots. Wreath-shaped or, rarely, bicycle-spoke patterns may occur. Well-defined hypoautofluorescent chorioretinal lesions are very atypical for primary MEWDS and are a relative exclusion criterion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document the distinctive individual lesions and support diagnosis, particularly in complex cases.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic imaging of active disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Lesions become apparent in the mid-phase as wreath-shaped or bicycle-spoke patterns, each with a hypofluorescent center encircled by hyperfluorescence; late leakage may occur. Optic nerve staining and focal or segmental periphlebitis are possible but nonspecific.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish MEWDS from other non-infectious posterior uveitis when diagnosis is challenging.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In selected diagnostically difficult cases rather than as a mandatory test for every case.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The early phase is usually normal or shows subtle changes. Hypofluorescent spots become clearer from the mid- to late phase and may persist after 20 minutes; smaller darker dots can overlie larger spots. Prominent early hypofluorescence attributable to choriocapillaris non-perfusion instead favors placoid chorioretinopathies and excludes MEWDS.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess retinal and choriocapillaris flow signal and help exclude MEWDS from the differential diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Retinal and choriocapillaris slabs usually retain their signal. A substantial reduction at the choriocapillaris level can serve as an exclusion criterion for MEWDS and is more indicative of a placoid-type condition.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate for syphilis as an alternative diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As part of excluding conditions that can resemble MEWDS.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Positive syphilis serology is an exclusion factor.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate for sarcoidosis as an alternative diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Evidence of sarcoidosis is an exclusion factor.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The lesions generally resolve spontaneously, although recurrence can occur. On serial imaging, OCT abnormalities improve, while FAF spots fade before their overlying dots.

conditions.name: secondary MEWDS
conditions.description: MEWDS-like lesions occurring alongside another primary condition, including PIC, MFC, neovascular AMD, or, less often, another disorder of the choriocapillaris-Bruch’s membrane–RPE complex.
conditions.clinical_presentation: MEWDS-like findings occur in the setting of an underlying disorder. A well-defined hypoautofluorescent chorioretinal lesion or bilateral presentation may prompt consideration of secondary disease, but neither finding alone establishes it.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess MEWDS-like lesions and possible underlying chorioretinal disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When findings raise the possibility of secondary rather than primary MEWDS.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Imaging features alone cannot fully resolve the distinction. The experts did not reach consensus on whether a chorioretinal scar present initially excludes primary MEWDS, and they considered the evidence insufficient for definitive imaging recommendations for secondary MEWDS.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify lesions that are atypical of primary MEWDS.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of suspected MEWDS-like disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A well-defined hypoautofluorescent chorioretinal lesion should prompt consideration of a masquerading condition or secondary MEWDS.

document_sections.heading: PURPOSE
document_sections.content: The report aims to establish imaging-based, expert-consensus guidance for using multimodal imaging in multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS).

document_sections.heading: DESIGN
document_sections.content: The guidance was developed through expert agreement informed by published literature and a nominal group technique (NGT).

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: An expert committee used repeated structured discussions, conflict resolution and anonymous voting to develop criteria for diagnosing and monitoring MEWDS with color fundus photography (CFP), optical coherence tomography (OCT), fundus autofluorescence (FAF), fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) and OCT angiography (OCTA). Illustrative MEWDS cases informed recommendations on assessing specific disease features. The full task force subsequently voted on those recommendations.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: Acute MEWDS is supported by characteristic CFP findings, multifocal disruption of the ellipsoid/interdigitation zone with hyper-reflectivity in the outer retina above it on OCT, and hyperautofluorescent spots on short-wave blue or green FAF. In diagnostically difficult cases, wreath-like FFA lesions and the absence of early ICGA hypofluorescence help distinguish MEWDS from other chorioretinopathies. A lack of characteristic choroidal OCT abnormalities and preserved OCTA signal in retinal and inner choroidal slabs provide further diagnostic support.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: Multimodal imaging is considered essential to diagnose MEWDS and distinguish it from other forms of non-infectious uveitis. The proposed imaging features extend the Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) classification, permit more detailed assessment of activity and provide insight into disease pathogenesis.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Jampol et al first described MEWDS in 1984 as a posterior uveitis affecting predominantly young women. Its incidence is approximately 0.22 per 100,000 people per year, without a significant racial or ethnic predilection. Typically unilateral gray-white outer-retinal spots may merge; their reported size is 50-200 µm. The disorder usually resolves without treatment within about 2 to 3 months, with visual acuity returning to normal or nearly normal. Recurrence is possible but uncommon. Approximately 95% of patients attain visual acuity of 20/25 or better after the acute phase. Its cause is uncertain. A post-viral immune response or auto-inflammatory process has been proposed because approximately half of affected people recall a preceding flu-like illness. The SUN Working Group developed classification criteria intended primarily to form a homogeneous research population, prioritizing specificity over sensitivity. Those criteria combine multifocal deep gray-white retinal spots and foveal granularity, usually unilateral and involving the outer retina; characteristic FFA hyperfluorescence arranged like a wreath or bicycle spokes, or OCT hyperreflective lesions extending from the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) into and/or through the ellipsoid zone (EZ) and outer nuclear layer (ONL); and absent or mild anterior chamber and vitreous inflammation. Syphilis and sarcoidosis must also be excluded. Under the SUN criteria, simultaneous bilateral onset almost universally rules out MEWDS. Broader availability of multimodal imaging (MMI) motivated diagnostic guidance on its use and interpretation. MMI helps distinguish disease entities and assess their features. The international Multimodal Imaging in Uveitis (MUV) task force developed MMI-based refinements to SUN classification for 5 conditions previously grouped as white dot syndromes; this report addresses MEWDS.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The International Uveitis Study Group (IUSG) initiated MUV to standardize imaging criteria for diagnosing and managing noninfectious posterior uveitis. Separate expert groups addressed individual conditions, using a structured NGT consensus process. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki; no clinical information or patient identifiers were shared. Vanderbilt University Medical Center granted an Institute Review Board exemption (IRB #240146).

document_sections.heading: MEWDS COMMITTEE SELECTION
document_sections.content: The MEWDS committee comprised 8 experts in uveitis and medical retina selected for their publications on uveitis, particularly MEWDS, and their experience with retinal imaging and related disease management. Members contributed to the literature review, case collection, image assessment, repeated discussions and consensus votes. The subcommittee reviewed published research before starting the study.

document_sections.heading: LITERATURE REVIEW AND CASE COLLECTION
document_sections.content: The literature review identified characteristic MEWDS findings across imaging modalities. The subcommittee agreed to use at least 15 illustrative cases. Eligible cases required a confirmed MEWDS diagnosis and a complete imaging set acquired within 2 to 3 weeks of symptom onset, during the acute phase. Cases with competing possible diagnoses, especially syphilitic posterior placoid chorioretinitis, were excluded. Members contributed cases from clinical archives worldwide. Selection did not rely on imaging alone: SUN classification criteria informed confirmation through clinical features, including absent or mild anterior chamber or vitreous inflammation; imaging findings, including wreath-like FFA lesions; and laboratory assessment, including exclusion of syphilis and sarcoidosis. Because MEWDS lacks a definitive biomarker, case selection could not be fully independent of imaging-based diagnostic criteria. Review by the full expert subcommittee was intended to limit individual selection bias.

document_sections.heading: TABLE 1. Key Research Questions for Standardizing the Diagnostic Process of Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome
document_sections.content: The table sets out the committee's research questions: whether imaging can define MEWDS as an entity; which findings across color fundus photography, optical coherence tomography, fundus autofluorescence, fluorescein angiography, indocyanine green angiography and optical coherence tomography angiography distinguish active MEWDS from other non-infectious posterior uveitic entities or argue against it; what demographic, laterality, clinical-course or laboratory information supplements imaging; and how secondary MEWDS appears clinically and on imaging.

document_sections.heading: NOMINAL GROUP TECHNIQUE
document_sections.content: Committee members examined CFP, FA, ICGA, OCT, FAF and OCTA from the selected cases. One subcommittee member, MM, facilitated without directing the decisions. Members proposed imaging features and discussed their diagnostic value. They held 3 virtual round-robin discussion rounds in which each member could contribute without interruption, discussion or criticism during the initial exchanges. Features lacking preliminary agreement were reconsidered using a questionnaire developed after the literature review. Anonymous voting followed the third round once remaining disagreements had been addressed.

document_sections.heading: ESTABLISHMENT OF FINAL CONSENSUS
document_sections.content: The subcommittee drafted imaging recommendations for diagnosis and monitoring. The wider MUV task force, comprising 49 members with varied geographic and subspecialty backgrounds, reviewed them through an online platform and discussed proposed changes. Members then voted anonymously. Agreement was classified as unanimous consensus at 100%, strong consensus at >95%, consensus at 75-95%, majority agreement at >50-75%, and no consensus at <50%; guidance receiving <50% was rejected. These thresholds followed guidance from international associations, including Guidelines International Network (GIN), European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) and Association of Scientific Medical Associations of Germany (AWMF). Study data were managed in REDCap at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. REDCap supports validated data entry, audit trails, export to statistical software and integration with external systems.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: The results describe modality-specific imaging appearances of MEWDS and present the imaging guidance and recommendations developed by consensus.

document_sections.heading: MULTIMODAL IMAGING FEATURES OF MEWDS (TABLE 2)
document_sections.content: The consensus imaging features span CFP, OCT, short-wavelength FAF, FFA, ICGA and OCTA. Their diagnostic value depends in part on disease phase and on whether a finding supports MEWDS or instead suggests another condition.

document_sections.heading: Color Fundus Photography
document_sections.content: On CFP, lesions appear as scattered, deep, faint grayish-yellowish-white spots, typically 50-200 µm across. They often spread outward from the posterior pole beyond the arcades into the midperiphery, but may be concentrated around the optic disc, macula or arcades and may coalesce. They fade without intervention, sometimes within days to weeks. Despite an otherwise subtle fundus appearance, unilateral foveal granularity is important and requires high-resolution color imaging to see reliably. Blurring of the involved optic disc can occur. An illustrative left-eye photograph obtained 1 week after symptoms began shows faint scattered white spots and foveal granularity.

document_sections.heading: TABLE 2. Imaging-Based Consensus Guidelines for Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome
document_sections.content: The table summarizes the imaging findings agreed for each modality: the distribution and fading of visible lesions and foveal granularity on CFP; EZ/IZ disruption and outer-retinal hyper-reflectivity on OCT; phase-dependent hyperautofluorescent spots and dots on short-wavelength blue or green FAF; characteristic mid-phase FFA lesions with possible late leakage; ICGA lesions that become more apparent later; and preserved retinal and choriocapillaris OCTA signal.

document_sections.heading: Optical Coherence Tomography
document_sections.content: During acute MEWDS, OCT shows multifocal alteration and attenuation of the interdigitation zone (IZ) and EZ. Focal EZ/IZ disruption with reduced reflectivity commonly accompanies hyper-reflective material, described as puff balls or pillars, extending from the EZ into the outer retina. Foveal involvement is frequent. Peripapillary EZ/IZ disruption can correspond to an enlarged blind spot. The external limiting membrane (ELM) may be attenuated or preserved. Occasional vertical foveal hyperreflective lines extend from outer-retinal bands to the inner retina. RPE, choriocapillaris and choroidal changes are not typical on OCT, although recurrent MEWDS can rarely show RPE irregularities. Vitreous hyper-reflective foci or cells and thickening of the peripapillary or macular retinal nerve fiber layer may occur but are nonspecific; peripapillary serous retinal elevation is rare. On en face OCT, EZ and IZ slabs can show characteristic hypo-reflective spots corresponding to EZ loss, with hyper-reflective dots above them. Spots fade before dots, and the appearance normalizes without intervention. OCT B-scans suffice for accurate diagnosis; en face OCT may supply further detail and confirmation. Near-infrared reflectance imaging, commonly provided with OCT B-scans, often shows wreath-like hypo-reflective lesions measuring 50-200 µm, particularly very early in the disease. An illustrated OCT series includes an initial visit after 1 week of symptoms and images at 2 weeks and 6 weeks, showing that the EZ/IZ abnormalities diminish over time.

document_sections.heading: Fundus Autofluorescence
document_sections.content: The subcommittee assessed short-wavelength blue and green FAF at 488 and 530 nm. FAF detects characteristic MEWDS spots more sensitively than CFP, although very early FAF may appear unremarkable. Acute disease shows punctate hyper-FAF spots of varying intensity with smaller hyper-FAF dots above them. A wreath-like, or rarely bicycle spoke-like, arrangement may also appear on FAF. Spots measure 50-200 µm and commonly spread outward from the posterior pole beyond the arcades into the midperiphery. During recovery, spots resolve before the dots. Hypo-FAF lesions are very atypical of primary MEWDS. Clearly defined hypo-FAF corresponding to chorioretinal lesions should raise consideration of a masquerading condition or secondary MEWDS and is a relative exclusion criterion for primary disease. Appearances may differ with excitation wavelength, filters and other imaging settings. An illustrated series at baseline, 2 weeks, 6 weeks and 3 months shows hyperautofluorescent spots giving way to smaller dots that subsequently fade; baseline images of 2 other cases show the distribution beyond the arcades.

document_sections.heading: Fundus Fluorescein Angiography
document_sections.content: FFA abnormalities are subtle in early frames, whereas the characteristic lesions emerge in the mid-phase and may leak in late frames. Individual wreath-like or bicycle spoke-like lesions have a hypofluorescent center bordered by circular hyperfluorescence, sometimes formed by a cluster of dots. Optic nerve staining and focal or segmental vasculitis, including periphlebitis, may occur but are nonspecific. Illustrative early, mid and late images show the characteristic borders and later leakage; another series shows optic nerve staining and segmental vasculitis during the mid and late phases.

document_sections.heading: Indocyanine Green Angiography
document_sections.content: Early ICGA is usually normal in MEWDS. Prominent hypofluorescent lesions at this stage, caused by choriocapillaris (CC) non-perfusion, are characteristic of placoid chorioretinopathies and exclude MEWDS. By the mid-to-late phase, hypofluorescent lesions are readily visible, spreading outward from the posterior pole, sometimes past the arcades into the midperiphery. Some devices show darker dots within larger spots. The smaller dots correspond to OCT hyper-reflective puff balls or pillars; the larger spots correspond to reduced reflectivity and disruption of EZ/IZ. Hypofluorescent lesions can remain visible in the very late phase, after 20 minutes. Their persistence helps distinguish MEWDS from Vogt-KoyanagiHarada disease and sarcoid choroiditis, in which choroidal lesions such as granulomas fade late. Illustrated ICGA frames show subtle early findings and spots present from the mid-phase through the late phase.

document_sections.heading: Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography
document_sections.content: OCTA is optional in MEWDS. Retinal and CC slabs ordinarily show no substantial signal reduction. OCTA can nevertheless help remove MEWDS from the differential diagnosis: a marked CC-level signal reduction favors placoid-type disease and can serve as an exclusion criterion.

document_sections.heading: CONSENSUS-BASED RECOMMENDATIONS
document_sections.content: The MEWDS subcommittee drafted recommendations that the MUV task force reviewed and voted on. CFP for recording lesion pattern and location received consensus, 94.7%; high-resolution CFP for assessing foveal granularity in active MEWDS received consensus, 81.6%. OCT for diagnosing active disease from outer photoreceptor layer changes received unanimous consensus, 100%, while OCT for excluding active MEWDS when substantial choroidal involvement is present received consensus, 92.1%. FAF, including ultra-wide field imaging, for diagnosis while accounting for wavelength-dependent variation received strong consensus, 97.4%. FFA for documenting characteristic individual wreath-like lesions in the mid-phase of active disease received consensus, 89.5%. ICGA to distinguish MEWDS from other non-infectious posterior uveitis when diagnosis is difficult received consensus, 81.6%. OCTA for documenting preserved flow signal in retinal and choriocapillaris slabs during active disease received consensus, 84.2%. Serial OCT and FAF follow-up received strong consensus, 97.4%. The 7 members of the expert subcommittee did not vote on these recommendations. The subcommittee also discussed secondary MEWDS, in which MEWDS-like findings accompany another primary disorder.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: The authors regard the standardized MMI criteria as a way to improve diagnosis and management while extending the SUN classification. The proposed exclusion features broadly align with published MEWDS findings. Minimal or absent anterior chamber and vitreous inflammation matters diagnostically; positive treponemal syphilis testing and evidence of sarcoidosis are additional reasons to exclude primary MEWDS. SUN treats simultaneous bilateral disease as exclusionary, but the expert group did not emphasize laterality over imaging. Published bilateral cases suggest bilaterality alone does not rule out MEWDS, although it is highly atypical and should prompt suspicion of a masquerading or secondary condition. The group's analysis located primary MEWDS chiefly in the outer retina, with overt RPE involvement rare and confined to recurrent cases; SUN instead allows RPE involvement, outer-retinal involvement or both. The group further characterized each FFA wreath-like or bicycle spoke-like lesion by a hypofluorescent center inside a sometimes dot-like hyperfluorescent ring. It agreed that prominent early ICGA hypofluorescence or marked CC-slab OCTA signal loss indicates substantial CC non-perfusion, typical of placoid chorioretinopathies rather than MEWDS. Although some reports suggest choroidal non-perfusion can vary in MEWDS, especially in severe disease, most cited literature supports treating CC non-perfusion as an exclusion criterion. Imaging findings in MEWDS vary, so the criteria aim to standardize most assessments without replacing clinical judgment in atypical cases. In particular, hyper-FAF spots vary across short-wavelength blue and green systems, prompting debate about mandatory findings. ICGA use in atypical presentations was also debated. Some members emphasized its value against placoid chorioretinitis; the experts agreed that early ICGA usually changes little or not at all, whereas the literature also describes early-to-mid-phase hypofluorescence. ICGA was ultimately retained as an additional test for selected clinical situations. The subcommittee did not specifically make ultra-wide field (UWF) imaging part of its core consensus criteria, despite its usefulness for peripheral retinal abnormalities in other uveitic disorders. Some studies suggest it may make MEWDS lesions easier to see and improve diagnostic sensitivity. The project instead prioritized broadly available OCT, FAF, FFA, ICGA and OCTA features; prospective assessment of the added value of UWF imaging remains necessary. The criteria chiefly address primary MEWDS. Secondary MEWDS can produce similar lesions with underlying PIC, MFC, neovascular AMD or, less often, other disorders of the choriocapillaris-Bruch’s membrane–RPE complex. Imaging alone may not resolve those diagnostic distinctions, and vitreoretinal lymphoma can also masquerade as MEWDS. Experts did not reach consensus on whether an initial chorioretinal scar excludes primary MEWDS. They considered secondary MEWDS a relatively new concept with insufficient evidence for definitive MMI recommendations and called for studies comparing primary and secondary disease. The authors identify the project's broadly applicable, standardized approach, international specialist participation and structured NGT conflict resolution as strengths. They also acknowledge that imaging alone is often insufficient for diagnosis, geographic and ethnic variation may affect prevalence and presentation, experts from some regions did not participate, and foveal granularity may be less frequent in some settings. Clinical features and other diagnostic information remain necessary. The criteria require validation in broader posterior uveitis cohorts, ideally prospective multicenter studies assessing sensitivity, specificity, true positives, true negatives and inter-rater reliability. Machine learning, as previously applied in the SUN project, might further improve robustness and generalizability. The authors conclude that consensus-based imaging standardization offers a framework for MEWDS diagnosis and management that can support patient care and broader uveitis practice.
